South Australian Parliament gets a taste of Deepavali, Annakut

By
Our Reporter
-
15/10/2026
0
66
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:25
Instaread

A Deepavali and Annakut reception was held at Parliament House in Adelaide on 14 October, bringing Hindu cultural traditions and their message of peace, gratitude and harmony to the wider Australian community.

Hosted by South Australian Minister for Multicultural Affairs Nadia Clancy MP, the event was attended by representatives of the Hindu Council of Australia’s South Australian Chapter.

The reception showcased the traditions and spiritual values associated with Deepavali, also known as Diwali, and Annakut, a Hindu festival of gratitude and devotion. The celebrations highlighted themes of light, hope, unity and harmony.

The Hindu Council of Australia’s South Australian Chapter thanked Ms Clancy for hosting the event and acknowledged the support of BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha Adelaide and the Hindu Organisations, Temples and Associations Forum of South Australia.

The chapter said it remained committed to promoting Hindu culture, encouraging interfaith understanding and strengthening multicultural harmony across South Australia.

The reception comes ahead of Adelaide’s Biggest Deepavali Festival, which is scheduled to take place at the Adelaide Showground. The festival is expected to bring communities together through cultural performances, traditional festivities and family entertainment.

Further details and ticket information are available through the event’s Eventbrite page.

Support Independent Community Journalism

Dear Reader,

The Indian Sun exists for one reason: to tell stories that might otherwise go unheard.
We report on local councils, state politics, small businesses and cultural festivals. We focus on the Indian diaspora and the wider multicultural community with care, balance and accountability. We publish in print and online, send regular newsletters and produce video content. We also run media training programs to help community organisations share their own stories.

We operate independently.

Community journalism does not have the backing of large media corporations. Advertising revenue fluctuates. Platform algorithms change. Costs continue to rise. Yet the need for credible, grounded reporting in a multicultural Australia has never been greater.

When you support The Indian Sun, you support:

• Independent reporting on issues affecting migrant communities
• Coverage of local and state decisions that shape daily life
• A platform for small businesses and community groups
• Media training that builds skills within the community
• Journalism accountable to readers

We cannot cover everything, but we work to cover what matters.

If you value thoughtful reporting that reflects Australia’s diversity, we invite you to contribute. Every donation helps us maintain the quality and consistency of our work.
